title: WhatsApp Head Kunal Shah Pledges Simpler App, Stronger AI Help
excerpt: In his first detailed note in the job, Kunal Shah sets three priorities — simpler voice, groups and video, everyday tasks finished inside a chat, and AI that tracks bookings and appointments — with no launch dates yet.
body:
• WhatsApp head Kunal Shah, who took over development leadership from Will Cathcart earlier this year, says the app used by more than 3 billion people has grown complex and will be made simpler.
  • His three priorities are richer connections (voice notes, groups, stickers and video made simpler and more expressive), everyday tasks finished inside the app, and AI that finds information and tracks bookings and appointments.
  • WhatsApp is working with financial services and telecom partners so paying a bill, borrowing money or staying connected while travelling feels as simple as sending a message.
  • For readers: nothing changes in the app today — Shah announced no launch dates and named no partners, so these are plans, not features you can use yet.

WhatsApp's new head has set out his plan for the messaging app: make it simpler to use, let people finish everyday tasks without leaving a chat, and give its artificial intelligence a larger, quieter role in keeping track of daily life.

Kunal Shah, who took over leadership of the app's development from Will Cathcart earlier this year, shared the note on Tuesday, titled as his thoughts five months into the role. According to TechCrunch, which published Shah's full note, WhatsApp is now used by more than 3 billion people but has grown complex as it packed in communities, channels, stories and business features that many users find hard to navigate.

First Priority: Richer, Simpler Connections

Shah's first priority is the core messaging experience itself. People send more than 10 billion voice messages and more than 4 billion stickers on WhatsApp every day, according to his note, and he said the company will make voice notes, groups, stickers and video "simpler and more expressive" as the way people communicate evolves.

"I think of WhatsApp like a shared language, spoken by 3bn+ people. Sometimes we use words, and sometimes it's a voice note to a parent, a sticker that ends an argument, or a 'home safely' at 2am."

— Kunal Shah, Head of WhatsApp

ANI, reporting Shah's post on X, added platform-wide figures from his message: more than 100 billion messages and 2 billion calls handled daily. For diaspora families, those groups, voice notes and video calls are often the main line to relatives in India.

Second Priority: Finishing Tasks Inside the Chat

The second priority extends WhatsApp further beyond messaging. "Too many things start in a chat and end with many more steps somewhere else: paying a bill, borrowing money, staying connected when you travel," Shah wrote. "Each handoff to another task costs time. We're working with financial services and telecom partners so that finishing something feels as easy as starting it."

TechCrunch noted that WhatsApp has long tried to build an ecosystem for exploring products and making purchases, and that Shah's note hints at more of that work, including partnerships that could enable bill payment, loans and eSIM purchases for travel. Shah did not name the financial or telecom partners, and he gave no launch dates for any of the services mentioned.

Third Priority: AI That Tracks What Matters

The third priority is artificial intelligence. Shah said AI should help inside the flow of ordinary use: "It should quietly find what you need, get things done and make sure you never miss a booking or an appointment. The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter."

WhatsApp already offers an AI assistant that can summarize messages and create drafts, TechCrunch reported. It is not clear, TechCrunch added, whether the company will use its Muse agent to collate information and send reminders to people. Shah described the goal — surfacing important information and helping users complete tasks — without announcing a specific new assistant or a rollout timetable.

Trust Message, and What Has Not Changed

Shah closed by stressing that the expansion would not change WhatsApp's founding promises. "Whatever we build, WhatsApp must remain simple, reliable and private," he wrote, adding that personal messages and calls stay end-to-end encrypted and that "that isn't changing." ANI reported the same assurance, quoting Shah: "Trust takes years to earn and a moment to lose, and I don't take it lightly."

What happens next is, for now, a watch item rather than an action item. There are no new features to download, no partner services to sign up for and no dates to mark. Readers should treat messages claiming to offer new WhatsApp loans or booking services as unverified until WhatsApp itself launches them. The direction is clear: fewer steps, more services inside the chat, and AI in the background.
nri_angle: WhatsApp group chats, voice notes and video calls are the main daily link between diaspora families and relatives in India, so Shah's simplification and AI plans directly affect how those families communicate.
author: Diaspora Desk
